title: The strong-side outlet closes
objective: Reassess an outlet when a forechecker occupies its side.
briefing: YOU control the puck beside Navy’s net on its centre-ice side. Gold 1 is near the direct lane to W. D2 is across the middle on the other side of the net. This drill permits a reverse if its route is available; it is not an automatic instruction. Navy defends the left net and attacks the right net.
cues: D2 is across the middle from YOU.
Gold 1 is near the direct route to W.

questions.prompt: Which teammate is on the opposite side of the net from YOU?

options.text: Gold 1
D2
W

questions.explanation: D2 and YOU are on opposite sides of Navy’s net.

questions.prompt: Select two checks before using the permitted reverse.

options.text: Whether D2 is ready
Whether the first planned pass must be completed
Whether pressure can reach the reverse route

questions.explanation: The reverse is an option only if its receiver and route remain usable.

questions.prompt: Arrange a possible reverse decision.

options.text: Assess pressure near the strong-side outlet
Check and communicate with D2
Use the reverse only if that route remains available

questions.explanation: The routine supports a decision, not an automatic reverse every time pressure appears.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to an example spot for protecting possession while looking toward D2.
questions.explanation: A tighter position toward the middle of the net can change the angle you present to pressure. Actual goalie and defender locations still matter.

questions.prompt: If D2 is closely marked before you release, what is sensible?

options.text: Reverse automatically because it was the original plan
Pass through D2’s marker without checking
Reassess a hold or another outlet

questions.explanation: A closed second option means another read is needed; holding may be useful if possession can be protected.

questions.prompt: Why is “the first outlet is closed” insufficient by itself to choose a reverse?
questions.explanation: A different lane and a prepared receiver must also exist. Mention pressure on D2 or time to protect the puck.

questions.prompt: What should YOU check with Gold 1 near the route to W?

options.text: Whether the direct W outlet is usable
D2 must own the puck
The puck is already in the neutral zone

questions.explanation: Gold 1 is near the direct lane to W. Check reach and movement before judging whether that lane is usable.

questions.prompt: Which two details should accompany a reverse call?

options.text: Which side D2 is on
Whether the reverse lane is open
That D2 is automatically open because Gold 1 is near W

questions.explanation: Communicate D2’s side and whether the proposed route is usable. Keep the call accurate as pressure changes.

questions.prompt: Move YOU toward an example behind-net position to reassess pressure and D2.
questions.explanation: The example moves the carrier and puck behind the goal line, beside the back of the net. Recheck the net, boards and pressure; the position does not prove a safe skating or passing route to D2.

questions.prompt: Why does a closed strong-side outlet permit a reverse without requiring it?
questions.explanation: The closure removes one lane while D2’s side and pressure determine whether the reverse helps; if the reverse is covered too, protect or wait.

title: Step out of the forechecker’s shadow
objective: Create a visible receiving option for a defender.
briefing: Navy D1 has the puck. YOU are a wide support player near the blue line. Gold 1 is close to the direct passing route. Navy C is closer to the defended left net and nearer the middle. Reoffer support if a usable lane is available.
cues: Gold 1 is close to the direct route to YOU.
C is a navy inside support option.

sources.title: U13 Skills — Core Skills
sources.section: Page 1, individual tactics and team play
sources.use: Supports age/topic placement only. The setup, alternatives and suggested answers are original experimental coaching synthesis, not source-certified.

limits: Age adaptation and tactical alternatives await coaching review. Static setup: no skating speed, interception timing or uniquely optimal route has been validated. Positional references are examples, not scored targets.

questions.prompt: Who currently owns the puck?

options.text: D1
YOU
C

questions.explanation: The puck is assigned to D1, so this question is about support without possession.

questions.prompt: Which two changes might make your support more useful?

options.text: Stay hidden behind Gold 1 until the pass arrives
Show a ready stick after scanning
Adjust the receiving angle

questions.explanation: Moving and preparing can help D1 see an option; any new location still needs a lane check.

questions.prompt: Arrange a way to reoffer along this wall.

options.text: Assess Gold 1 near the passing route
Move to change the passing angle
Look back and prepare to receive

questions.explanation: The order is a suggested support routine rather than a fixed skating pattern.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to a different receiving angle from D1.
questions.explanation: Coming off the boards can separate the passing route from Gold 1. Check C’s space rather than crowding it.

questions.prompt: If Gold 1 follows your inward move, which response could help?

options.text: Call for a pass without looking at Gold 1
Reoffer elsewhere or make room for C
Remain still because your first move should have worked

questions.explanation: A supporter should update the option; the first movement does not guarantee availability.

questions.prompt: How can your movement help D1 even if D1 passes to C?
questions.explanation: Explain how moving Gold 1 or clearing a route can help another teammate. Receiving the puck is not the only useful outcome.

questions.prompt: Which passing route is Gold 1 closest to?

options.text: The lane between D1 and YOU
The route from C to Navy’s net
The far blue-line exit

questions.explanation: Gold 1 is close to the D1-to-YOU route. An angle change may help, but the new lane still needs checking.

questions.prompt: Which two calls help D1 use your movement?

options.text: Say when you are clear of the shadow
Identify C’s inside support
Call “I’m open” and leave D1 to guess your new angle

questions.explanation: Communicate actual availability and C’s support position. A short clear call can work; it must match the current lane.

questions.prompt: Move YOU toward the middle to compare a receiving angle from D1.
questions.explanation: The example moves YOU inward and changes the passing angle. It does not prove visibility or reception; recheck Gold 1 and C.

questions.prompt: How can movement help D1 even if the puck goes to C?
questions.explanation: Stepping off the direct lane can pull Gold 1 and open C or D1’s next route; if the defender ignores you, D1 can use the space you created.

title: Offer a deeper middle regroup option
objective: Provide a deeper middle option during a neutral-zone reset.
briefing: Navy D1 holds the puck just behind the defensive blue line. YOU are F2 in the neutral zone; F1 is farther up ice and wider. The coach asks YOU to offer an option closer to Navy’s net and nearer the middle, while checking the gold defenders.
cues: D1 has the puck behind the defensive blue line.
The coach asks F2 to offer deeper middle support.

sources.title: U15 / U18 Practice Plan — High Performance Practice 4
sources.use: Supports the stated coaching principle. The setup, alternatives and suggested answers are original experimental coaching synthesis, not source-certified.

limits: Adapted down from the U15/U18 drill to a slower U13 support read; no original diagram is copied. Static setup: no skating speed, interception timing or uniquely optimal route has been validated. Positional references are examples, not scored targets.

questions.prompt: Which supporting role does the coach give F2?

options.text: Deeper middle support
A stationary spot beside F1
A rush directly to the far net

questions.explanation: The role is stated in the briefing and is not inferred from a system name.

questions.prompt: What two features could make F2’s option different from F1’s?

options.text: Matching F1’s exact position
A more central angle
A position closer to Navy’s net

questions.explanation: Different depth and angle can create another choice; a defender may still close it.

questions.prompt: Arrange a possible regroup support routine.

options.text: Notice F1’s position farther up ice
Offer a deeper middle target
Adjust as D1 chooses a route

questions.explanation: The support routine is flexible and should respond to the puck.

questions.prompt: Move YOU into a deeper middle support example.
questions.explanation: This location gives D1 a different depth from F1. Check Gold 1 before treating it as a passing lane.

questions.prompt: Gold 1 moves directly onto your new lane. What might you do?

options.text: Rush beside F1 and remove the deeper option
Change the angle again or help clear F1’s route
Demand the same pass regardless

questions.explanation: An option should be re-created when the marker moves.

questions.prompt: Why can two forwards at similar depth make D1’s options easier to defend?
questions.explanation: They may be covered by similar pressure and leave no release toward their own net. Spacing depends on defenders, not just symmetry.

questions.prompt: What could YOU call before moving closer to Navy’s net than F1?

options.text: I will offer middle support closer to our net
I will match F1’s height
The far net is open

questions.explanation: State the planned support angle and recheck availability. A call does not make the passing lane open.

questions.prompt: Which two facts make a deeper route useful?

options.text: F1 is already farther up ice and wide
The coach has asked for a different passing angle
YOU and F1 should overlap

questions.explanation: The assigned depth and middle angle can offer another option if the route is usable.

questions.prompt: Move YOU closer to Navy’s net than F1 and toward the middle.
questions.explanation: This example changes depth and width, but brings YOU closer to Gold 1. Recheck pressure rather than assuming the connection is safer.

questions.prompt: When might different depths give D1 more options?
questions.explanation: Different depths can create distinct passing angles if both remain reachable. One defender does not automatically cover both players at the same depth, and staggering does not guarantee an open route.

title: The point shot has a blocker
objective: Compare the current shooting lane with another angle.
briefing: YOU have the puck high in the zone. Gold 1 is directly between YOU and the net. D2 offers a lateral option while F1 is near the far side. Navy attacks Gold’s net and defends Navy’s net. This is a selected-player teaching view; no movement is implied unless stated.
cues: Gold 1 shares the centre lane between the puck and the attacking net.
YOU have the puck high in the zone. Gold 1 is directly between YOU and the net. D2 offers a lateral option while F1 is near the far side.

sources.use: Supports the stated coaching principle. The setup, alternatives and suggested answers are original experimental coaching synthesis, not source-certified.

limits: Age adaptation and tactical alternatives await coaching review. Static setup: no skating speed, interception timing or uniquely optimal route has been validated. Positional references are examples, not scored targets.

questions.prompt: Who stands on the straight line from YOU toward the net?

options.text: F1
Gold 1
D2

questions.explanation: Gold 1 shares the centre lane between the puck and the attacking net.

questions.prompt: Choose two ways to investigate a different shooting opportunity.

options.text: Look for a lateral angle
Assume the puck must go through Gold 1
Check whether D2 has a usable connection

questions.explanation: Moving or passing may change the lane; this picture alone does not prove a shot will reach the net.

questions.prompt: Order one response to the blocked point lane.

options.text: Notice Gold 1 in the lane
Check movement and passing options
Use the option that remains available

questions.explanation: A player may choose a pass, carry or shot depending on the next cue.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to compare a lateral shooting angle.
questions.explanation: A small lateral change shifts the line to the net. Check whether Gold 1 can follow before treating it as open.

questions.prompt: Suppose Gold 1 follows your lateral move. What deserves another look?

options.text: The original shot as though Gold 1 had stayed still
A shot without checking the blocker
A pass to D2 or another change of angle

questions.explanation: A moving defender can close the new lane, so alternatives remain relevant.

questions.prompt: Why does “move sideways” not guarantee a clear shot?
questions.explanation: Explain that the blocker, other players and goalie can also adjust.

questions.prompt: Which teammate can give YOU a lateral puck option if Gold 1 stays in the shooting line?

options.text: D2
Gold 1
The goalie

questions.explanation: D2 is a Navy teammate at a different lateral angle. Check the route and receiver before passing; Gold 1 may adjust.

questions.prompt: Which two changes could alter the shooting picture?

options.text: D2 moves laterally
YOU change the puck’s angle to the net
Shoot without checking the blocker

questions.explanation: Moving the carrier or finding a lateral pass can change the shooting line. Recheck the blocker and goalie before choosing.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to compare another puck angle toward the net.
questions.explanation: YOU carry the puck to the example point. It shifts the shooting line slightly and moves closer to Gold 1; neither a clear shot nor a pass to D2 is guaranteed.

questions.prompt: Why does a blocker make the read about geometry rather than simply shooting harder?
questions.explanation: Gold 1 occupies the direct line, so angle, screen and support determine what is visible; if those do not change, more force does not create a lane.

title: Offer again after a short pass
objective: Recognize a useful off-puck movement after passing.
briefing: YOU have just passed to F2. Gold 1 faces F2 near the boards. You are still in the place from which you passed; the exercise asks you to seek another visible option. Navy attacks Gold’s net and defends Navy’s net. This is a selected-player teaching view; no movement is implied unless stated.
cues: The puck is now assigned to F2 after the stated pass.
YOU have just passed to F2. Gold 1 faces F2 near the boards. You are still in the place from which you passed; the exercise asks you to seek another visible option.

sources.use: Supports age/topic placement only. The setup, alternatives and suggested answers are original experimental coaching synthesis, not source-certified.

limits: Age adaptation and tactical alternatives await coaching review. Static setup: no skating speed, interception timing or uniquely optimal route has been validated. Positional references are examples, not scored targets.

questions.prompt: Which player is the new puck carrier?

options.text: F2
YOU
Gold 2

questions.explanation: The puck is now assigned to F2 after the stated pass.

questions.prompt: Which two reads help before reoffering?

options.text: Whether the return pass is guaranteed
The space available beyond your old spot
The defender’s attention and position

questions.explanation: A give-and-go needs a real route and a prepared carrier, not just a memorized pattern.

questions.prompt: Arrange one reoffer routine.

options.text: Confirm the pass arrived
Scan the next support space
Move and become visible again

questions.explanation: The route should change if the defenders remove the expected opening.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to illustrate a new inside option for F2.
questions.explanation: Moving into different ice changes the passing picture. The reference is only useful if Gold 2 and Gold 1 cannot remove that route.

questions.prompt: If Gold 2 moves into your new route, what could you do?

options.text: Follow the route without looking
Change direction or stay as another support option
Insist on the return pass anyway

questions.explanation: The pass does not obligate the receiver to return it; another support action may be better.

questions.prompt: How can you judge whether your second movement improved the play?
questions.explanation: Look for a new useful route, space created for F2 or a defender moved—not only whether you received a return pass.

questions.prompt: What can YOU call to make F2 aware of your reoffer?

options.text: Inside option when you can see me
The first pass is still coming
No need to look at pressure

questions.explanation: The call names a new inside option while leaving F2 to confirm the lane; if Gold 1 tracks the route, re-space before asking for the puck.

questions.prompt: Which two cues should drive your second movement?

options.text: F2’s new puck position
Gold 1 facing F2
Your original spot staying fixed

questions.explanation: The new carrier location and defender orientation shape the return lane; staying fixed can leave you behind pressure.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to compare another passing angle for F2.
questions.explanation: The example changes the passing angle. It is farther from F2 than the starting spot, so it is not automatically a shorter release. Recheck both defenders before calling for a pass.

questions.prompt: How can YOU tell a reoffer is helping instead of just following the puck?
questions.explanation: It should change the passing angle and preserve separation from Gold 1, while keeping another teammate useful; if it closes every lane, re-space.
